extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism students, sociologists of media, and researchers analysing press/news production
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and production practices for moving from hard news to feature coverage and for composing feature articles (selection of background, sources, typographical form, balance/montage, ideological framing). Useful for analysing or producing newspaper feature pieces about crime/social problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic/sensational/novel elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatic/sensational/novel elements (i.e. length of sentence and type of crime)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensational facts (e.g. unusually long sentence, brutality of crime) supply the immediate hook for news and shape what is treated as 'hard' news; these elements are often foregrounded to produce attention and define newsworthiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Hard' news dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Hard' news dynamics stress immediate 'facts' and their implications (i.e. for general penal policy)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hard news treats the immediate event and its direct policy/administrative implications; it privileges concise factual reporting and a focus on how an event affects broader institutional questions (e.g. penal policy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness as ideologically conditioned
rubrics_metrics.description: The sense of what is 'news-worthy' derives from, and reinforces, an ideologically-charged conception of society
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors' and journalists' judgments about what is newsworthy are not neutral but reflect and reproduce wider ideological frameworks (e.g. seeing some neighbourhoods as 'problem areas'); analysts should examine how choices reinforce particular social conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of events as having a background
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of events as having a background not covered by hard news story (i.e. crime and criminal have a social background)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features are commissioned when an event is interpreted as symptomatic of wider social contexts; this shift legitimates investigation into causes, context and 'background problems' beyond immediate facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioning reporters to obtain reactions and accredited interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Commissioning reporter(s) to dig around for 'reactions' and interpretations by accredited sources (i.e. contacting those immediately involved and/or lobbyists and experts)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A production practice: features mobilise reporters to gather views from victims, local residents, lobby groups, academics, police and politicians; source selection shapes the angle and explanations offered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of background elements and exclusions
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting those background elements cum explanations considered relevant (i.e. not politico-judicial links nor drugs and violence, but Handsworth, its inhabitants and experts)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors choose which background elements to pursue — this selection (and omission) determines the frame and possible causal narratives; analysts should note what is excluded as well as included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Picking up and amplifying source cues of typicality
rubrics_metrics.description: Picking up cues provided by sources as to typicality of events or as symptomatic of underlying issues (e.g. Ethel Saunders and 'lousy area'; Handsworth MP and 'war against crime')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters often seize on source-provided typifications ('typicality' cues) to generalise from an incident to broader social problems; such cues can naturalise causal claims (area→crime, race→crime).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanation / contextualisation (placing events and actors on a 'map' of society)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanation/contextualisation: placing the events and the actors on a 'map' of society
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature value includes contextualising individuals and events within social structures (housing, employment, race relations); good features should make explicit the connections rather than merely list 'indices'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification and channeling of social issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Identification of social issues: channelling public concern (i.e. Handsworth as a 'problem area')
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature pieces select and amplify particular social problems (housing, unemployment, race) and thereby direct public concern; this is both a journalistic function and an ideological act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeking out relevant actors and locations
rubrics_metrics.description: Seeking out the actors and locations carrying the relevant experiences and quasi-explanations (i.e. the victim; the mugger; the police; the street or area)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical feature technique: include interviews/portraits of the victim, alleged perpetrator, police, local residents and settings to provide texture and authority to explanatory narratives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placing actors/locations in relation and typographical 'setting up'
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing the actors and locations in relationship to each other; 'setting it up' typographically; use of photographs and reporters' 'feel pieces'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features often construct meaning by juxtaposing portraits, photos and layout (double-page spreads, left/right contrasts); typographic design and image choices contribute to apparent balance and to ideological framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible solutions and policy recommendations as feature elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Possible solutions to defined problems (e.g. praise of voluntary work/police; calls for crash youth programme/research)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features commonly conclude or include suggestions for remedies (community projects, policing tactics, policy reform), which steer the discourse toward particular interventions and away from structural explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface coherence and manageability
rubrics_metrics.description: Surface coherence: pulling elements together into one focal point (e.g. Guardian's use of community worker's comment on sentence being as insensitive as the crime)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Features create a coherent, manageable story by synthesising diverse elements into a single focal argument or image — this makes complexity consumable but can flatten contradictions and obscure deeper causal links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reintegration into the paper's dominant discourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Reintegration of feature into paper's dominant discourse
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature explanations are often folded back into the editorial/political orientation of the newspaper (e.g. conservative papers emphasise law-and-order, liberal papers stress social policy), so feature content should be read in relation to the paper's broader stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing by montage (juxtaposition of competing readings)
rubrics_metrics.description: Balance by montage: juxtaposing a number of ways of interpreting the connection between crime and environment, biography and background
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A common strategy is to present multiple, often conflicting readings side-by-side (victim vs mugger; police vs community worker) to convey comprehensiveness; however, selection and placement can still tilt ideological weight despite formal balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature-by-microcosm strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature by microcosm effect: distilling general themes into a particular local instance
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some features treat a local story as emblematic of wider social trends (Handsworth as microcosm); this can illustrate broader issues but risks collapsing complexity into a single illustrative anecdote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of 'Neither-Norism' / equivocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivocation ('Neither-Norism'): stating two opposites and balancing them so as to reject them both (balancing to avoid choosing)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An editorial tendency that neutralises debate by formally balancing opposites without resolving or analysing them; critiques should note when balance is used to evade judgement rather than to illuminate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of one-dimensional language / cliche
rubrics_metrics.description: One-dimensional language: words and concepts tend to coincide; the word becomes cliche and, as cliche, governs the speech or the writing (Marcuse)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journalistic prose should avoid cliche-driven declarations that preclude qualification, negation or debate; such language impedes conceptual thought and masks ideological commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Source emphasis and ideological appropriation (victim focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of the victim (availability for interview, photograph) as privileged source which can be ideologically appropriated (justification of sentence)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Which sources are privileged (e.g. the victim's testimony, injuries, photographs) affects the interpretive balance; attention to availability and editorial use of such sources reveals ideological effects (e.g. re-legitimising punitive measures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and weighting of experts and authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Selection of experts (criminologists, MPs, councillors, police spokesmen) and the weight given to their views influences resolution of the feature's argument
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Which 'expert' voices are quoted, how long they are allowed to speak, and their placement shape the reader's conclusion; comparative analysis should track whose interpretations are amplified or marginalised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal layout can simulate balance while tilting ideology
rubrics_metrics.description: Typographical representation of balance (e.g. Express double-page: left Handsworth/mugger; right victim/appeal to police)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Layout and montage may create an impression of formal balance, but the rhetorical and discursive selection within those panels can produce a net ideological tilt; analysts must read form and content together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid listing symptoms without connecting causes (reject simplistic environment/behaviour model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid simplistic environment/behaviour model that enumerates indices of 'depression' (housing, unemployment, racial resentment) without providing connections or origins
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good feature work should attempt to explain causal linkages and structural origins (housing market, historical processes) rather than merely associating indices; mere description risks reproducing determinism and stereotyping.
